zones.name: Venus cloud layer
zones.who_owns: Nobody. The Outer Space Treaty bars any government from taking a planet by declaration, use or occupation. Nothing is built there, so no one has tested whether a balloon drifting in the air of Venus counts as a space object or as use of the planet.

rules.says: No government may appropriate a celestial body by declaration, use, occupation or any other means.
Private activity in space needs authorization and continuing supervision from a treaty state, and states answer for what their nationals do.
The state that launches a space object keeps jurisdiction and control over it.

zones.hook: Your launch needs a state's authorization on Earth, and that state keeps jurisdiction over the craft after it leaves.
zones.can_you_build: No one has. Every proposal is a paper study. The one NASA study received no further funding and was canceled by 2017. Soviet Vega balloons floated in the atmosphere only for days, until their batteries ran out.
facts: At 55 km: 27 C, 0.5 bar, gravity 8.73 m/s2 (NASA HAVOC figures)
At about 50 km: about 1 atm, 0 to 50 C (Landis figures)
Breathable air lifts in the CO2 atmosphere with over 60% of helium's lifting power on Earth
Cloud-top winds up to 95 m/s

zones.name: Moons and dwarf planets of the outer solar system
zones.who_owns: Nobody. Moons and dwarf planets are celestial bodies, so the Outer Space Treaty's ban on national appropriation applies. The pages retrieved for these proposals do not discuss ownership or law at all.

rules.says: No government may appropriate a celestial body by declaration, use, occupation or any other means.
Private activity needs authorization and continuing supervision from a treaty state.

zones.hook: A launching state keeps jurisdiction over your craft and must supervise private activity; the treaty summary retrieved states no distance limit. No craft has carried people there, so this has not been tested.
zones.can_you_build: No crew has been sent under any of these plans. NASA's own Callisto study assumed major propulsion advances for a round trip of about 2 to 5 years.
facts: Europa: unshielded radiation about 5.40 Sv per day; about 5 Sv over a few days is fatal
Ganymede: about 0.08 Sv per day, gravity about 0.15 g
Callisto: gravity about 0.13 g, outside Jupiter's radiation belt
Titan: gravity 0.138 g
Enceladus: subsurface ocean only tens of meters under the south pole ice

sources.t: Colonization of the outer Solar System (Wikipedia)

zones.name: The Sun
zones.who_owns: Nobody in law, though the treaty's wording names governments. Spanish claimant María Ángeles Durán argues the agreement stops countries from owning a star and leaves individuals free. The pages retrieved report no court ruling on that argument.

rules.says: Bars governments from appropriating a celestial body. Whether this reaches a private person is the point Durán disputes.

zones.hook: There is no way to reach the Sun, so the hook is on Earth: a notary, a sales platform's rules, and a local court.
zones.can_you_build: Nothing can be built. The only activity on record is paperwork and online sales of plots at one euro per square metre.
facts: Durán's notarial deed: 2010
Plots: 1 euro per square metre
Claim against eBay: 10,000 euros (The Register); about 7,500 pounds (Scottish Financial News)

sources.t: The Register, eBay Sun lawsuit, 5 June 2015
Excelsior, La dueña del Sol, 21 Jan 2022

zones.name: Interstellar and generation ships
zones.who_owns: A ship would stay under the jurisdiction of the state that launched it, according to the treaty summary retrieved, which states no distance at which that ends. No one has ruled on what happens to law on a voyage of many generations.

rules.says: The launching state retains jurisdiction and control over the space object.
Private activity needs authorization and continuing supervision by a treaty state, and states bear international responsibility for it.
States are liable for damage their space objects cause.

zones.hook: Private launches need authorization and continuing supervision from a treaty state under Art. VI. The Starshot page does not discuss launch approval, and no project retrieved has reached that stage.
zones.can_you_build: No. Only studies and paper designs exist for crewed ships. The one funded uncrewed probe plan, Breakthrough Starshot, was reported on hold indefinitely in September 2025.
facts: Alpha Centauri: 4.34 to 4.37 light-years
Starshot: US$100 million initial funding, about $4.5 million spent by 2025 per Philip Lubin
Project Persephone worldship concept: 20 km long, 5 km across, 50 to 500 people
DARPA gave 100 Year Starship $1M and NASA Ames $100K; the 2012 grant was $500,000
Outer Space Treaty: 118 parties as of October 2025

zones.name: Orbiting megastructures and space elevators
zones.who_owns: A structure in orbit belongs under the jurisdiction of the state that launched it. A space elevator would also touch Earth: its anchor sits on a state's land or at sea, and the Wikipedia page on the idea notes that oceanic anchors are often in international waters, which could simplify territory negotiations.

rules.says: The launching state retains jurisdiction and control over a space object.
States are liable for damage caused by their space objects.
Private activity needs authorization and continuing supervision by a treaty state.

zones.hook: Launch licensing and liability on Earth, plus for an elevator, whichever state or sea hosts the anchor.
zones.can_you_build: None has been built. The stated technical block for elevators is the cable: Google X froze its project in 2014 after finding no one had made a defect-free carbon nanotube strand longer than a meter. Voyager Station is already a separate entry on this map.
facts: Stanford torus: 1.8 km ring, 10,000 residents, about 10 million metric tons
Kalpana One (revised 2007): 250 m radius, 325 m long, 3,000 people
Bishop Ring (1997): 1,000 km radius, about 3 million km2 of land
McKendree cylinder (1995): 460 km radius, 4,600 km long
Obayashi: 8-day climber trip to geosynchronous orbit, target 2050

sources.t: Space habitat, reached from Kalpana One (Wikipedia)

zones.name: Airborne living and high-altitude platforms
zones.who_owns: Air over a country falls under that country's rules, and the pages retrieved give no case of anyone claiming a flying nation. In practice a platform answers to the aviation and radio authorities that certify it. The ITU treats a high-altitude platform as a radio station.

rules.says: Defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at 20 to 50 km, at a specified nominal fixed point relative to the Earth.
Ends at 60,000 ft; platforms fly above it. The page retrieved does not say how they are regulated up there.

zones.hook: Certification and flight authorization before takeoff, radio spectrum rules, and the need to land somewhere for maintenance. Stratobus plans a couple of days on the ground each year.
zones.can_you_build: Uncrewed platforms have flown; no one lives on one. Sky Cruise is a video concept. Several programs ended: Facebook Aquila was halted in 2018, Google Loon ended in 2021, and Titan Aerospace's Solara was shut down by 2017.
facts: HAPS band: 20 to 50 km
Stratobus: about 20 km, 100 m long, 5 tons, 250 kg payload
Helios reached 96,863 ft on 13 August 2001 and broke up in flight in 2003
Airbus Zephyr: 64-day endurance goal

sources.t: Thales Alenia Space, All about Stratobus
My Modern Met, Sky Cruise, 1 July 2022

zones.name: Countries with no land
zones.who_owns: Nothing is owned, because nothing is claimed on the ground or the claim is carried with the person or object. The people involved remain under the law of the place where they stand.

rules.says: Slowjamastan's founder cites these criteria as the basis of its legitimacy. The page retrieved does not list them, and it reports no legal recognition.

zones.hook: Your home country's law continues to apply. Lennon and Ono asked for diplomatic immunity. The page records no grant of it; his deportation order was overturned in 1975 and he received a green card in 1976.
zones.can_you_build: Anyone can declare one, and several have lasted decades as organizations. The pages retrieved report no recognition by any state.
facts: Nutopia's anthem: four seconds of silence
Obsidia's territory: two portable pieces of obsidian
Atlantium: almost 3,000 citizens as of 2015, most signed up online

cases.name: NASA HAVOC
cases.anchor: NASA Langley Research Center, Hampton, Virginia, where the study originated
cases.founder: Dale Arney and Chris Jones, NASA Langley
cases.story: HAVOC, short for High Altitude Venus Operational Concept, was created in 2014 by Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers in the Space Mission Analysis Branch at NASA Langley. A meeting about Mars habitation prompted the idea, and they published it at an American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics forum in Pasadena in 2015. The plan targeted 55 km above Venus, where the temperature is 27 C and pressure 0.5 bar. It ran in five phases: a robot airship 31 m long; astronauts in Venus orbit; a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 m long; a one-year stay; and last a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total. NASA later said HAVOC was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a true mission for human exploration. It received no further funding and was canceled by 2017, though some of its technologies were developed further for possible Moon and Mars missions.
cases.mechanism: A government study carries no claim: the permanent phase was never tested against the treaty ban on taking a celestial body.

cases.name: Geoffrey Landis's floating cities on Venus
cases.anchor: NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio, the author's institution
cases.story: Geoffrey Landis of NASA Glenn Research Center presented a paper called Colonization of Venus at a conference on human space exploration in Albuquerque in February 2003. He argued that the trouble with Venus is that its ground lies too far below the level of one atmosphere of pressure, so settlers should live in the air instead. At about 50 km up, pressure is near 1 atm and the temperature 0 to 50 C. An aerostat, meaning a craft that floats like a balloon, could use ordinary breathable air as its lifting gas, because air is lighter than the carbon dioxide around it. Landis's figure is over 60% of helium's lifting power on Earth. People outside would need breathable air, acid protection and some heat protection, with no pressure suit. A leak would mix slowly, leaving time for repairs. The structures would have to resist sulfuric acid. The atmosphere above would give radiation shielding equal to Earth's. Aerostats might in the extreme cover the whole planet. Nothing has been built.
cases.mechanism: Living in the air raises an open question the treaty does not answer directly: a drifting city occupies no fixed ground, yet Art. II bars appropriation by use or occupation of the planet.

cases.name: Floating Islands of Venus
cases.anchor: Moscow, placed only to mark the Soviet Union; the pages give no base
cases.story: In 1971 the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky proposed the Floating Islands of Venus, an early version of the idea of living in the Venusian atmosphere above its hostile surface. Another page retrieved confirms Soviet scientists were proposing atmospheric settlement at least as early as 1971. In 1991 Paul Birch suggested a related design, two-part domes filled with hydrogen or helium, in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society. None was built.
cases.mechanism: A design proposal only, made before the Moon Agreement and without any claim of ownership on the pages retrieved.

cases.name: Settling Titan
cases.anchor: Lakewood, Colorado, placed for Zubrin's base; this is from general knowledge, not the page
cases.story: Robert Zubrin, an aerospace engineer, wrote in Entering Space (1999) that Saturn is the most valuable of the gas giants and Titan the best moon for a base. His reasons, as summarized on the page: Saturn is relatively close, has low radiation and has a good moon system. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as an abode of life in Analog in 1992. Titan has a nitrogen and methane atmosphere that could supply a buffer gas for breathing air, and water beneath the surface that could yield oxygen. Radar studies published in 2008 by Ralph Lorenz's team found hundreds of times Earth's known oil and gas reserves in hydrocarbons. Lakes span about 1 km to 100 km. Objections include extreme cold, gravity of 0.138 g with unknown effects on bone, muscle and child development, and a lack of free oxygen for chemical power. Charles Wohlforth and Amanda Hendrix's Beyond Earth (2016) is listed in the page's bibliography. No one has sent a crew or a settlement plan beyond the paper stage.
cases.mechanism: Resource talk runs straight into the open debate over whether extraction counts as appropriation under Art. II.

cases.name: Artemis Project plan for Europa
cases.anchor: No base given on the page; coordinate left empty
cases.story: In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Jupiter's moon Europa. It proposed igloos on the surface as bases from which to drill through the ice and explore the ocean below, and it suggested people could live in air pockets inside the ice. Europa's hidden ocean may hold over twice the water of all Earth's oceans, but metals and minerals would have to be imported. Radiation is the main bar: an unshielded person would take about 5.40 sieverts a day, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. The page says heavy shielding might make a research base possible. The plan was not carried out.
cases.mechanism: A private plan would need a state's authorization and supervision under Art. VI, and none is recorded.

sources.t: Colonization of the outer Solar System (Wikipedia)

cases.name: NASA HOPE study for Callisto
aka: Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration
cases.anchor: NASA Headquarters, Washington DC; the page does not name the lead center
cases.story: In 2003 NASA ran a study named HOPE, for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration. It chose Jupiter's moon Callisto because Callisto orbits outside Jupiter's radiation belt. The base would sit on the surface and could produce fuel for further exploration of the solar system. Callisto has accessible water, silicate rock and metals, gravity of about 0.13 g, and probably an internal ocean. The estimated round trip for a crew was about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. The study remains a study.
cases.mechanism: A state base on a moon would be legal only as long as it does not amount to appropriation under Art. II.

sources.t: Colonization of the outer Solar System (Wikipedia)

cases.name: Ceres megasatellite world
cases.anchor: Helsinki, placed for the author; from general knowledge, the arXiv abstract page does not state it
cases.story: In a preprint first posted in November 2020 and revised in May 2021, Pekka Janhunen laid out a settlement in high orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt. He picked Ceres mainly for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires. Spinning habitats attached to a disk-shaped frame by magnetic bearings would give 1 g of artificial gravity, and mirrors would bring in sunlight. Population density would stay at 500 people per square kilometer, on soil 1.5 m deep, upgradable to 4 m. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material, mostly soil and radiation shielding. The stated aim is a long-lasting world with all atoms recycled. A space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply, which the author considers feasible given Ceres's low gravity and fast rotation. The paper is not listed with a journal reference on the arXiv page.
cases.mechanism: Building in orbit from mined material sits on the unsettled question of whether resource extraction is appropriation of a celestial body.

cases.name: María Ángeles Durán's claim to the Sun
cases.anchor: Vigo, Spain, the claimant's home
cases.challenge: eBay removed listings; lawsuit in Alcobendas court, outcome not found
cases.story: María Ángeles Durán of Vigo, Spain, obtained a notary's document in 2010 declaring her owner of the Sun, and threatened to charge solar power users. She argues that an international agreement stops any country from owning a planet or star, and that an individual is not bound by it. She then sold plots on eBay at one euro per square metre. About two years after she opened her account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods and blocked her account. She sued in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid. A June 2015 report said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, and Excelsior in 2022 says the court declared itself competent and gave her standing to sue. She sought 10,000 euros, and a first hearing was set for 17 June 2015. Excelsior in January 2022 dates legal recognition of her ownership to 2012, conflicting with the 2010 date, and cites no documents. None of the pages retrieved reports how the case ended, and a court allowing a suit to proceed is different from a court finding that she owns the Sun.
cases.mechanism: A notary recording a claim and a court accepting a consumer suit are procedural steps; neither page reports any court ruling that a person can own a star.

sources.t: The Register, eBay Sun lawsuit, 5 June 2015
Excelsior, La dueña del Sol, 21 Jan 2022

cases.name: Project Hyperion
cases.anchor: Technical University of Munich, Germany
cases.story: Project Hyperion studies crewed interstellar generation ships, meaning ships whose voyage lasts longer than a human life. Andreas Hein launched it in December 2011 out of WARR, a student group at the Technical University of Munich, as part of the Icarus Interstellar program. The team published World ships: architectures and feasibility revisited in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012 and presented results at a European Space Agency workshop in 2019. In 2014 Cameron Smith used Hyperion data to study how large a population must be to stay genetically viable. A design competition opened in 2024, with a cited CBC headline describing a 250-year journey. Results came in July 2025: first place went to the Italian Chrysalis team, second to Poland's WFP Extreme, third to Malaysia's Systema Stellare Proximum. The page does not discuss governance or name a destination. Core members later moved to the world ship project at the Initiative for Interstellar Studies.
cases.mechanism: A generation ship would remain under the launching state's jurisdiction on the treaty summary retrieved, so children born aboard would inherit a state's law from before their birth.

cases.name: Icarus Interstellar
cases.anchor: Alaska, state of registration; placed at Anchorage
cases.founder: Andreas Tziolas, Richard Obousy, Kelvin Long, Pat Galea, Adam Crowl
cases.story: Icarus Interstellar is a volunteer nonprofit, registered as a US 501(c)(3) in Alaska in February 2011. It grew from Project Icarus, a five-year study of a fusion starship launched in September 2009 by Kelvin Long and Richard Obousy, building on the British Interplanetary Society's 1970s Project Daedalus. Its stated mission is to realize interstellar flight before the year 2100, aiming at stars within 15 light-years or habitable planets within 22. Projects included Hyperion, Persephone, Forward, Tin Tin and Voyager. Persephone studied ecosystems for a worldship 20 km long and 5 km across, housing 50 to 500 people. A Starship Congress in Dallas in August 2013 drew nearly 200 people, and another was scheduled for September 2015 at Drexel University. The page reports nothing after 2015, so its current activity could not be confirmed.
cases.mechanism: A US-registered nonprofit would fall under US authorization and supervision through Art. VI if it ever launched.

cases.name: 100 Year Starship
cases.anchor: Houston, Texas, host of the 2012 to 2014 symposia
cases.cost: $1.1M seed from DARPA and NASA Ames; $500,000 grant in 2012
cases.story: The 100 Year Starship began in summer 2010 with David Neyland, a director at the US defense research agency DARPA, working with Paul Eremenko. NASA Ames director Pete Worden announced it in October 2010 before government coordination was complete, which caused friction. DARPA put in $1 million and NASA Ames $100,000. A January 2011 workshop in California listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate issues. The first symposium, in Orlando in 2011, drew over 700 people. In 2012 a consortium led by former astronaut Mae Jemison's Dorothy Jemison Foundation won a $500,000 grant and took over the name and DARPA's intellectual property. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful spending projects, citing a session called Did Jesus Die for Klingons Too? Symposia followed in Houston, Graz in 2015 and Nairobi in 2023, the last activity the page describes.
cases.mechanism: A government seeded the study and handed it to a private group, so any ship would still need a state's supervision under Art. VI.

cases.name: Breakthrough Starshot
cases.anchor: New York City, where it was announced
cases.story: Yuri Milner announced Breakthrough Starshot in New York on 12 April 2016, with Stephen Hawking; Mark Zuckerberg was also on the board. The plan is uncrewed: about 1,000 centimeter-sized probes weighing a few grams each, on sails up to 4 m by 4 m, pushed by ground-based lasers of up to 100 GW to 15 to 20% of the speed of light. They would reach Proxima Centauri b, 4.34 to 4.37 light-years away, in 20 to 30 years. Initial funding was $100 million, with Milner putting the final cost at $5 billion to $10 billion and a first launch around 2036. In September 2025 Scientific American reported the project on hold indefinitely, and Philip Lubin estimated about $4.5 million of the $100 million had been spent. The page reports no formal cancellation and does not discuss launch approval.
cases.mechanism: A 100 GW laser array on the ground would sit inside some state's territory, so the state hook would come before launch.

cases.name: Article VIII and a ship with no end distance
cases.anchor: UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, Vienna
cases.story: The Outer Space Treaty opened for signature on 27 January 1967 and entered into force on 10 October 1967. It has 118 parties as of October 2025. On the summary retrieved, the state that launches a space object retains jurisdiction and control over it, states are liable for damage caused by their objects, and private activity requires authorization and continuing supervision by a treaty state. That summary states no point at which jurisdiction ends. On that reading, a ship leaving the solar system would carry its launching state's jurisdiction indefinitely, and a person born aboard would be under that state's authority. The treaty also calls astronauts envoys of mankind. No court or agency has been recorded applying these articles to a voyage between stars.
cases.mechanism: Jurisdiction follows the object, with no distance limit stated in the summary retrieved, which is the closest thing to law on a generation ship.

cases.name: Stanford torus
cases.anchor: Stanford University, where the study was held
cases.story: In 1975 a NASA summer study at Stanford University worked up designs for space colonies, and its conclusions appeared in 1977 as Space Settlements: A Design Study. Its wheel-shaped habitat, the Stanford torus, has a ring about 1.8 km across with a living tube 130 m wide, for 10,000 permanent residents. It turns once a minute to give 0.9 to 1.0 g of artificial gravity. It would have about 10 million metric tons of material, and about 95% of that is radiation shield. The site is the Earth-Moon L5 point. It was never built. A 2012 paper adapted it for a generation ship.
cases.mechanism: A settlement in free space would be built on no celestial body, so Art. VIII on jurisdiction matters more for it than the Art. II ban on taking one.

cases.name: Bishop Ring
cases.anchor: No base given on the page; coordinate left empty
cases.story: Forrest Bishop of the Institute of Atomic-Scale Engineering proposed this rotating ring in his 1997 paper Open Air Space Habitats. It would have a radius of about 1,000 km and a width of 500 km, with walls about 200 km high to hold in the air and no roof. The living area of about 3 million square kilometers is close to the size of Argentina or India. It relies on carbon nanotubes, the material that lets it be far larger than the steel O'Neill designs of the 1970s. Bishop considered sites at the Sun-Earth L4 and L5 points, closer to the Sun, and the asteroid belt or beyond. It remains hypothetical.
cases.mechanism: A habitat that size would still count as a single space object under its launching state's jurisdiction, if a state licensed it at all.

sources.t: Space habitat, reached from Kalpana One (Wikipedia)

cases.name: Kalpana One
cases.anchor: No base given on the page; coordinate left empty
cases.story: Kalpana One is a space settlement design revised in 2007 by Al Globus, with a radius of 250 m, a length of 325 m, and a population of 3,000. Its shielding runs at 10 metric tons per square meter and rotates with the habitat. It is one of a family of concepts listed on the same page, among them Lewis One, also by Globus, and the 1995 McKendree cylinder with a radius of 460 km. The page says no space settlement has been built, and adds that the L4 and L5 points once favored are now thought too far from the Moon and Earth, with a two-to-one resonance orbit proposed instead.
cases.mechanism: Any such settlement would fall under the jurisdiction of the state that launched it, under Art. VIII.

sources.t: Space habitat, reached from Kalpana One (Wikipedia)

cases.name: Obayashi space elevator
cases.anchor: Obayashi head office, Tokyo
cases.story: In 2012 the Japanese construction company Obayashi announced it could build a space elevator by 2050 using carbon nanotubes. A passenger climber would reach geosynchronous orbit in an 8-day trip. It published further details in 2016, and the page cites a 2018 report on a tiny first step, without further outcome. The material remains the main obstacle: a 2016 study by Feng Ding's team suggested flaws could sharply cut nanotube strength, and Google X put its own elevator project in deep freeze in 2014 after finding no one had made a defect-free strand longer than a meter.
cases.mechanism: An elevator is tied to Earth at its base, so the host state or the high seas at the anchor point would set the terms before any space law applied.

cases.name: Edwards ribbon and the sea anchor
cases.anchor: Estimated point in the western equatorial Pacific; the proposal names no exact spot
cases.story: From 2000, Bradley Edwards worked on a thin ribbon elevator of carbon nanotube composite under NASA's advanced concepts institute, with more than 20 institutions and 50 participants. He suggested anchoring it in the western equatorial Pacific to avoid lightning and hurricanes, on a movable sea anchor so it could dodge debris that can be tracked. His plan began with a 19,800 kg seed cable and added material with 207 climbers, reaching about 750 tons with a 20-ton lift per climber. The page notes oceanic anchors are often in international waters, which could simplify territory negotiations, and quotes Philip Ragan saying the first country to deploy an elevator could control most space activities.
cases.mechanism: Placing the base on the high seas is the proposal's way of avoiding a host state, though the launching state's duties remain.

cases.name: LiftPort Group
cases.anchor: Millville, New Jersey, the announced plant site
cases.story: LiftPort Group announced in 2005 a carbon nanotube plant in Millville, New Jersey, with a goal of launching a space elevator in 2010. In February 2006 it reported testing a mile of carbon fiber and fiberglass tether, about 5 cm wide and 1 mm thick, held up with balloons. In April 2019, CEO Michael Laine admitted little progress had been made despite over $200,000 in seed funding. The 2005 plant was never built.
cases.mechanism: The company never reached a stage where any state's approval was tested.

cases.name: Stratobus
cases.anchor: Thales Alenia Space, Cannes, France; site from general knowledge
cases.story: Stratobus is a robotic airship designed by Thales Alenia Space of France, selected by the French Ministry of Industry under its New Industrial France program. It would hold station at about 20 km, above the jet stream and regular air traffic. It is 100 m long, 33 m across, about 5 tons, with up to 250 kg of payload and 5 kW of power. Its planned life is five years, with a couple of days a year on the ground for maintenance, and it would reach the stratosphere in under four hours from a site the size of a football field. Thales's interview dated 22 May 2015 planned a prototype in 2018 to 2019, and commercial sale around 2020. That page says flight testing must be completed before certification and flight authorization. The page mentions no people aboard, and later milestones could not be confirmed in the pages retrieved.
cases.mechanism: The airship needs certification and flight authorization before it flies, so a state controls it before altitude becomes a question.

sources.t: Thales Alenia Space, All about Stratobus

cases.name: Sky Cruise
cases.anchor: No base given on the page; coordinate left empty
cases.story: Sky Cruise is a concept for a nuclear-powered flying hotel, released as an animated video by Hashem Al-Ghaili in mid-2022. The original design came from art director Tony Holmsten, who drew it over a decade earlier. It would carry up to 5,000 people and stay aloft for years, with passengers and supplies arriving from airports around the world on commercial and private jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili cited small nuclear reactors expected in the 2030s as a possible source of power. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly. Al-Ghaili himself stressed it is just a concept.
cases.mechanism: A craft that never lands would still depend on jets from licensed airports, and would raise the question of whose flag it flies under.

sources.t: My Modern Met, Sky Cruise, 1 July 2022

cases.name: ITU definition of a high-altitude platform
cases.anchor: ITU headquarters, Geneva
cases.story: The ITU, the UN agency for radio spectrum, defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at 20 to 50 km and at a specified, fixed point relative to the Earth. The definition sits in the ITU Radio Regulations at paragraph 1.66A. The band sits above US Class A airspace, which ends at 60,000 ft. Programs inside this field include Airbus Zephyr, BAE PHASA-35, Kea Atmos Mk1 and Stratobus. The page does not say how such platforms are licensed by national authorities.
cases.mechanism: This is a radio rule, and it says nothing about who owns the air at 20 to 50 km, so the band is defined for spectrum only.

cases.name: Barbados metaverse embassy
cases.anchor: Bridgetown, capital of Barbados
cases.recognition: Barbados itself only; no other state reported
cases.story: On 14 November 2021, Barbados's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade signed an agreement with Decentraland, a virtual world with over 90,000 parcels of land bought with cryptocurrency. Gabriel Abed, a crypto entrepreneur and Barbados's ambassador to the UAE, brokered the deal. The embassy could launch around January 2022 and would offer services such as e-visas. Avinash Persaud, special envoy to Prime Minister Mia Mottley, called it the first official embassy or lookout post in the metaverse, and promised a report in twelve months. If launched, Barbados would be the first country to formally recognize digital sovereign land. A CoinDesk opinion piece called the metaverse element a gimmick and asked why a website would not do. Global Voices does not state the embassy's legal status, how many parcels Barbados bought, or the cost. Whether the embassy opened and the report appeared could not be confirmed from the pages retrieved.
cases.mechanism: A government recording virtual land as sovereign changes nothing under diplomatic law unless other states accept it, and the page reports no such acceptance.

sources.t: Global Voices, Barbados embassy in the metaverse, 29 Nov 2021

cases.name: Decentraland parcels
cases.anchor: Buenos Aires, placed for the founders' Argentine origin; the city is from general knowledge
cases.cost: $2.43M highest plot sale on the page, Nov 2021
cases.story: Decentraland is a virtual world created by Argentine developers Ari Meilich and Esteban Ordano, begun in 2015. It raised $26 million in a 2017 coin offering and opened to the public on 20 February 2020. Land is sold as tokens on the Ethereum blockchain, paid for with the MANA currency. The first map, Genesis City, has 90,601 parcels, sold at about $20 each at launch. Prices reached $6,000 to $100,000 in April 2021, and a company paid $2.43 million for a plot in November 2021. Governance runs through a community vote and a nonprofit foundation. In November 2021 a vote on banning the name Hitler failed to reach enough votes to take effect. Use stayed small: DappRadar found fewer than 1,000 users a day making transactions in October 2022.
cases.mechanism: Owning a token gives a right inside one platform's rules, with no land under any state's law.

cases.name: Liberland in the metaverse
cases.anchor: Liberland's claimed land near the Serbia-Croatia border
cases.challenge: Croatia controls access to the land
cases.recognition: None; Serbia and Croatia dismiss the claim
cases.story: Zaha Hadid Architects, under principal architect Patrik Schumacher, planned a virtual world for Liberland, the unrecognized state declared in 2015 by Czech activist Vít Jedlička on land near the Serbia-Croatia border. Renderings show curving buildings, a City Hall, a DeFi Plaza and a central plaza. The stated aim is to support Liberland's development and serve as a hub for Web 3.0 and crypto developers, while also working as a standalone virtual realm. Schumacher argues open metaverses run by their communities will beat those run by corporations. Serbia's foreign ministry has called Liberland a frivolous act needing no further comment. The article gives no launch date, no land sales, and no status beyond the renderings.
cases.mechanism: A virtual city gives a state with no physical access a place to gather, without changing the claim's legal position on the land.

sources.t: Artnet News, Zaha Hadid Architects and Liberland

cases.name: Edge Esmeralda
cases.story: Edge Esmeralda is a month-long pop-up village in Healdsburg, California, about an hour north of San Francisco, organized by the Edge City team and described as a spin-off of Vitalik Buterin's Zuzalu. Its 2024 edition drew about 1,300 people. The P2P Foundation page calls it the first explicitly family-friendly pop-up village and says it aimed to seed a nearby permanent village named Esmeralda. It runs under ordinary California and local law.
cases.mechanism: A gathering in a US town stays under US law, so the experiment is in social organization and raises no sovereignty question.

cases.name: Vitalia
cases.story: Vitalia was a longevity-focused pop-up village held in February 2024 in Próspera, Honduras. The village included a biohacking lab, workout groups, and a biomedical hackathon, and the organizers intended it to seed a permanent home base. It appears in lists of Zuzalu spin-offs.
cases.mechanism: It used a zone with its own legal regime to host experiments, so its standing depends on Honduras's treatment of Próspera.

cases.name: Zuitzerland
cases.anchor: Center of Switzerland; the directory names no site
cases.story: The Network State Atlas directory lists Zuitzerland as a pop-up city in Switzerland working on decentralized leadership models and an integrated network society. It gives no year, site or attendance. No other page retrieved described it, so this entry is limited to its name, country and stated aim.
cases.mechanism: A gathering inside Switzerland operates under Swiss law.

cases.name: ShanhaiWoo
cases.anchor: Chiang Mai, Thailand, October 2024 gathering
cases.story: ShanhaiWoo appears on an Agartha list of pop-up cities as located in China and Thailand, and IOSG's report lists it among the communities in Chiang Mai in October 2024. Neither gives founders or attendance.
cases.mechanism: A temporary gathering operates under the law of the host country.

cases.name: Crypto Valley, Zug
cases.story: Zug, a Swiss town of 30,934 residents at the end of 2020, is called Crypto Valley because of its many cryptocurrency companies, among them Ethereum, Cardano, Polkadot and Bitcoin Suisse. In 2016 the town began accepting digital currency for small fees up to 200 francs, converting it into Swiss francs straight away to reduce risk. A Crypto Valley Association had formed by 2018, with Oliver Bussmann as president. A 2021 Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung article reports taxes in the canton could be paid in Bitcoin. Zug remains an ordinary part of Switzerland.
cases.mechanism: Here a local government adopted a technology inside national law; it claims no separate status.

cases.name: Nutopia
cases.anchor: 1 White Street, Manhattan, the first embassy address
cases.story: John Lennon and Yoko Ono announced Nutopia at a press conference in New York City on 2 April 1973, a day after signing its declaration. Its text says Nutopia has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people, and no laws other than cosmic ones. Citizenship came from declaring awareness of it. All citizens were ambassadors, and the founders asked for diplomatic immunity and UN recognition. Lennon had just received a deportation order, and the country was partly a way to address that. Its flag was a white handkerchief, and its anthem, on Lennon's 1973 album Mind Games, is four seconds of silence. The embassy was an apartment at 1 White Street in Manhattan, later a plaque on a kitchen door at the Dakota. Lennon's order was overturned in 1975 and he received a green card in 1976. Since April 2024 people can declare citizenship through a website.
cases.mechanism: Declaring a country to seek immunity brought no recorded immunity; Lennon's position changed when the deportation order was overturned in 1975.

cases.name: Global Country of World Peace
cases.anchor: No location given on the page
cases.story: Maharishi Mahesh Yogi founded the Global Country of World Peace in 2000 as a borderless nation for peace. Its attempts to buy territory failed, and Tony Nader led it as of 2023. Its currency has limited acceptance.
cases.mechanism: Failed land purchases left an organization with no territory, so it functions as a membership body.

cases.name: Nova Roma
cases.anchor: No location given on the page
cases.story: Nova Roma, founded in 1998, is an organization recreating classical Roman society through ancient religion, reenactments and its own coins. Some people count it as a micronation.
cases.mechanism: It operates as a voluntary organization, with no land claim on the page.

cases.name: Ambulatory Free States of Obsidia
cases.anchor: No fixed location, by design
cases.story: Carolyn Yagjian founded Obsidia in 2015 as a mobile feminist micronation and art project. Its territory is two portable pieces of obsidian. It promotes gender equality and LGBTQ rights.
cases.mechanism: A portable territory is a claim that travels with objects, and the law of wherever they sit continues to apply.

cases.name: Empire of Austenasia
cases.anchor: Sutton, London
cases.story: The Empire of Austenasia, founded in 2008, is based in a house in Sutton, London. It claims to succeed the Roman Empire, and its territory has grown to include small properties around the world as citizens joined.
cases.mechanism: Adding private properties by agreement of owners moves no border and changes no law on those plots.

cases.name: Grand Duchy of Avram
cases.anchor: Hobart, Tasmania, from general knowledge; the page says only Australia
cases.story: The Grand Duchy of Avram dates from the 1980s in Australia. It claims no territory and operates as a micronational bank. Its founder, John Charlton Rudge, faced several lawsuits, and a court eventually found he had committed no crimes.
cases.mechanism: A bank without territory is tested on commercial and criminal law, and here the founder was cleared.

cases.name: Russian Empire / Imperial Throne / Romanov Empire / Arca Noë
cases.anchor: No fixed location on the page
cases.story: Anton Bakov founded this project in 2011 and renamed it in 2014 and 2016. It claims former territories of Russia. By 2020 its plans turned to artificial islands in the Mediterranean, under the name Arca Noë.
cases.mechanism: The move to artificial islands repeats the plan to build on open water; the page reports nothing built.

cases.name: Empire of Atlantium
cases.anchor: Province of Aurora; placed by estimate from 'about 350 km southwest of Sydney'
cases.founder: George Cruickshank, Geoffrey Duggan, Claire Coulter
cases.story: Three Sydney teenagers founded the Empire of Atlantium in 1981, with the claim dated 27 November. George Cruickshank became head of state as Emperor George II. The group went quiet around 1990 and revived in 1999. Its capital moved from a 10 square meter provisional territory in Narwee to a 61 square meter apartment in Potts Point, Sydney, and on 12 January 2008 to the Province of Aurora, 0.76 square kilometers of land about 350 km southwest of Sydney. Almost 3,000 citizens were on its rolls in 2015, from over 100 countries, most signed up online and never visited. It sold coins, stamps and banknotes in an imperial solidus of 100 centi and appointed unaccredited legates in about ten countries. The page notes that it is mainly non-territorial, that both properties stay under Australian law, and that no state recognizes it.
cases.mechanism: Buying land gave a base, without any change in the law on it: Australian jurisdiction continues.

cases.name: Kingdom of Tavolara
cases.story: Tavolara is an island off northeast Sardinia. The Bertoleoni family claims it as one of the world's smallest kingdoms, allegedly sanctioned by King Charles Albert of Sardinia; the infobox dates the claim to 1836. Giuseppe's son became King Paolo I in the 1840s and reigned until 1886. Italy paid 12,000 lire in 1861 for land on the island for a lighthouse, which began operating in 1868. After 1886 newspapers reported a republic with a president and council, a report the page treats as unconfirmed. Carlo I died in 1928, and Mariangela, aunt of the absent Paolo II, ruled as regent until her death in 1934, which is said to have left the kingdom to Italy. A NATO station was installed in 1962, the year Paolo II died. Tonino Bertoleoni, head of the family, runs a restaurant on the island and the family keeps the claim.
cases.mechanism: A family's claim rests on an alleged royal sanction, and Italy treated the island as its own in buying the lighthouse land and hosting NATO.

cases.name: Kingdom of North Dumpling
cases.story: Inventor Dean Kamen, known for the Segway, bought two-acre North Dumpling Island in Fishers Island Sound in 1986 for $2.5 million. It lies in the town of Southold, New York, about a mile off Connecticut. Local officials refused his request for a wind turbine, and he declared secession from the United States, though he later got permission for the turbine. He calls it the Kingdom of North Dumpling, with a constitution, a flag, a currency named the dumpling, an anthem and a navy of one amphibious vehicle. Kamen says his friendship with President George H. W. Bush produced an unofficial non-aggression pact; the page records this only as his claim. The island runs on its own wind and solar power and holds an 1859 lighthouse. The secession has no legal recognition.
cases.mechanism: A joke secession to protest a denied turbine permit; the island remains part of the United States and of Southold, New York.

cases.name: Great Republic of Rough and Ready
cases.founder: Rough and Ready mining settlers, company led by Capt. A. A. Townsend
cases.story: Rough and Ready, California, was settled in fall 1849 by a Wisconsin mining company led by Captain A. A. Townsend, who named it after General Zachary Taylor. On 7 April 1850 the town declared secession from the Union as the Great Republic of Rough and Ready, largely to avoid mining taxes. It voted to rejoin less than three months later, on 4 July. The town still celebrates the republic each year for tourism and local pride. Its population was 905 in the 2020 census.
cases.mechanism: Secession in a remote mining camp lasted only until residents voted to rejoin; no federal case was needed.

cases.name: Sovereign State of Winneconne
cases.founder: Vera Kitchen and Winneconne Chamber of Commerce
cases.story: Wisconsin's 1967 highway map left off the village of Winneconne, showing only a blank little circle. The village feared losing tourist money. Governor Warren Knowles said the map could not be redrafted and promised a fix in 1968. Chamber of Commerce president Vera Kitchen ran a contest called Here's How to Put Winneconne Back on the Map, drawing over 1,000 entries. Two congressional aides in Washington won with a plan for secession and war. The village kept the secession, delivered a declaration to the governor on 22 July 1967, lowered the state flag and raised a banner with a skunk, sheepshead fish, poison ivy and a dodo. Parades, boat races and a one-day toll bridge followed. Knowles phoned that day with the state's regrets, and the secession lasted under 24 hours. The village has celebrated Sovereign State Days nearly every year since.
cases.mechanism: A publicity secession ended by a phone call, with no legal claim ever pressed.

sources.t: Wisconsin Life, How a tiny Wisconsin village went viral

cases.name: Killington's votes to leave Vermont
cases.story: Voters in Killington, Vermont, a town of 1,407 in the 2020 census, have twice approved the idea of leaving Vermont to join New Hampshire. Some residents feel the town gets too little back for the taxes it sends the state. The page calls the votes largely symbolic: the move would need approval from both state legislatures and the US Congress. It gives no dates or vote counts.
cases.mechanism: Moving a town between states needs both legislatures and Congress, so a local vote alone has no effect.

cases.name: Murrawarri Republic
cases.anchor: Weilmoringle, New South Wales, site of the first council meeting
cases.founder: Peoples Council of the Murrawarri; Fred Hooper
cases.challenge: Case taken to the UN, 12 May 2013
cases.recognition: None; Australian government has not acknowledged it
cases.story: The Murrawarri people released a declaration of independence on 30 March 2013, covering land across the Queensland and New South Wales border. They sent it to Queen Elizabeth II, Prime Minister Julia Gillard and the two state premiers. It asked for one of three things: treaty documents with the Crown, a deed of cession showing the Murrawarri gave up sovereignty, or documents declaring war on them. The Crown did not reply by the deadline of 8 May 2013, and the council read that silence as confirming continued independence. Time reported that the Attorney-General's Department did not respond because it had no legal basis to do so, a view Sydney human-rights lawyer George Newhouse backed. A Provisional Council of State first met on 13 July 2013 at Weilmoringle, chaired by Fred Hooper. The website claims 81,796 square kilometers, while a 2018 study put the area near 22,170. It uses Australian currency.
cases.mechanism: The claim rests on the absence of any treaty or cession from Aboriginal peoples, and asks the Crown to produce one.

cases.name: Sovereign Yidindji Government
cases.anchor: Cairns, Queensland, inside the claimed area
cases.founder: Murrumu Walubara Yidindji, Gudju Gudju Gimuybara
cases.challenge: Queensland traffic charge, May 2015; outcome not reported
cases.story: The Yidindji group renounced legal ties with Australia in 2014; the list of micronations gives 2013. Gudju Gudju Gimuybara is chief minister and Murrumu Walubara Yidindji foreign and trade minister. Its claimed land covers about 2,500 square kilometers south of Port Douglas, through Cairns and inland across the Atherton Tablelands, plus 80 km of sea. It issues its own driver's licences. In May 2015, Queensland police charged Murrumu after finding him with a licence and plates from the Yidindji government; he argued the police have no jurisdiction over him, and the page reports no outcome. It launched a digital Sovereign Yidindji Dollar in 2022, pegged to the Australian dollar. It hopes for a memorandum with the Commonwealth and has approached Russia and Venezuela.
cases.mechanism: Using its own licences brought the claim into a traffic charge, the point where Australian courts meet the assertion of sovereignty.

cases.name: Ganienkeh
cases.anchor: Altona, New York
cases.laws: Community meetings; alcohol and recreational drugs banned
cases.challenge: Tax auction of 11 parcels, final ruling for the county 2025
cases.story: In May 1974 traditionalist Mohawks occupied Moss Lake, a girls' camp near Old Forge, New York, claiming it as historic territory and sending a manifesto to the UN and President Nixon. The armed occupation ended in 1977 after nearly 200 negotiating sessions, with a move to land at Miner Lake near Altona, leased through the Turtle Island Trust. The state Court of Appeals upheld the lease in 1981, and it has run month to month since 1992. Residents call Ganienkeh an independent North American Indian state, and relations with New York have never been defined. In 1990 a rifle shot traced to the area wounded a doctor on a Vermont National Guard helicopter, and an 11-day armed standoff followed with no arrests. Businesses include tax-free bingo, cigarettes and an unlicensed casino. Clinton County auctioned 11 trust parcels in 2012 over about $300,000 in back taxes, and a 2025 ruling favored the county.
cases.mechanism: Negotiation with a state produced a lease, with sovereignty left undefined; courts have since ruled against the trust on back taxes.

cases.name: Kalakuta Republic
cases.story: After returning from the United States in 1970, Nigerian musician Fela Kuti declared his compound at 14 Agege Motor Road, in the Mushin area of Lagos, independent from the military-run state. It housed his family and band, a recording studio and a free health clinic. On 18 February 1977, a thousand armed soldiers attacked and the compound burned to the ground. Fela's mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a second-floor window and died after about eight weeks in a coma. On 15 October 2012 a Kalakuta Republic Museum opened after a rebuilding effort led by Governor Babatunde Fashola.
cases.mechanism: A military state answered a symbolic independence claim with force, leaving no legal case to test it.

cases.name: Free Republic of Wendland
cases.stopped_by: Lower Saxony police and Federal Border Guard, 4 June 1980
cases.story: On 3 May 1980 anti-nuclear activists occupied drilling site 1004 near Gorleben, West Germany, the site studied for nuclear waste storage, and proclaimed the Free Republic of Wendland. About 5,000 people took part, with around 1,000 staying permanently. They built about 110 huts of wood and clay, a Friendship House, greenhouses, an infirmary and a sauna. The information center issued a Wendenpass for 10 marks, said to be valid for the entire universe so long as its owner could still laugh. Radio Free Wendland began pirate broadcasts on 18 May. The state interior minister called the proclamation high treason. On 4 June, on Chancellor Helmut Schmidt's orders, about 3,500 police and border guards cleared the camp, with about 2,000 occupiers holding a largely peaceful sit-in. A 30th anniversary in 2010 drew about 800 people.
cases.mechanism: Occupying a state-planned site led to a police clearance, and treason was the charge named by a minister.

cases.name: Principality of Outer Baldonia
cases.anchor: Tusket Islands, Nova Scotia
cases.story: American businessman Russell Arundel founded Outer Baldonia in 1949 on about 4 acres of Outer Bald Tusket Island, the southernmost of the Tusket Islands off Nova Scotia, and took the title Prince of Princes. Its charter, kept at the Yarmouth County Museum, covered 69 fishermen. Soviet state publication Literaturnaya Gazeta criticized the charter, and on 9 March 1953 Outer Baldonia declared war on the Soviet Union. Press coverage later showed it was a humorous half-truth. Arundel sold the island in 1973 for one Canadian dollar to the Nova Scotia Bird Society, and in 2015 the Bald Islands were donated as conservation lands.
cases.mechanism: A private fishing club used a charter and titles on land it owned under Canadian law, and the claim lapsed with the sale.

cases.name: Slowjamastan
cases.story: DJ Randy Williams visited the Republic of Molossia in August 2021, bought 11.07 acres of Imperial County desert in California for $19,000 that October, and declared independence on 1 December 2021. He calls himself sultan and describes a dictatorship with occasional democracy. A border sign and post stand by State Route 78, with a desk as the sultan's office. It has no inhabitants, as of February 2025, and more than 25,000 citizens, as of March 2026, who apply online. Passports carry quotations from hip hop artists and the currency is the duble. Williams grounds its legitimacy in the Montevideo Convention criteria. It has no legal recognition.
cases.mechanism: Private ownership of land gives the use of it, while California and US law continue to apply.

cases.name: Principality of Snake Hill
cases.anchor: New South Wales center; the page names no site
cases.story: In 2003 a family in New South Wales, Australia, that could not afford its taxes declared secession as the Principality of Snake Hill.
cases.mechanism: A declaration made over a tax bill; the page gives no state response.

cases.name: Principality of Islandia
cases.anchor: Near Belize City; Coffee Cay position estimated
cases.story: The Principality of Islandia was crowdfunded in 2018 and claims Coffee Cay, an uninhabited island near Belize City.
cases.mechanism: A crowdfunded claim on an island that sits inside Belize.

cases.name: Glacier Republic
cases.anchor: Southern Patagonian ice field, placed by estimate
cases.story: In 2014 Greenpeace declared Chile's ice sheets a micronation to draw attention to weak legal protections for glaciers.
cases.mechanism: A campaign tactic using statehood language to push for a domestic law.

cases.name: Other World Kingdom
cases.anchor: Černá, Czech Republic; position estimated
cases.story: Other World Kingdom, founded in 1996 at Černá in the Czech Republic, was a BDSM resort in a château that claims to be an independent female-dominant matriarchy.
cases.mechanism: A private business using the language of statehood.

cases.name: Kingdom of Wallachia
cases.anchor: Moravian Wallachia, placed at Vsetín
cases.challenge: Leadership dispute in a Czech court
cases.story: Founded as a joke in Moravian Wallachia in the Czech Republic in 1997. A dispute over leadership reached a Czech court.
cases.mechanism: A joke state ended up in court on who ran it, showing Czech law applied to it throughout.

cases.name: Principality of Aigues-Mortes
cases.story: In 2010 the French city of Aigues-Mortes named itself a principality as a publicity stunt, based on a local legend about a royal title.
cases.mechanism: A city government's tourism stunt, with no change in French law.

cases.name: Principality of Laàs en Béarn
cases.story: In 2015 the French commune of Laàs declared itself a principality and seceded, alleging neglect by the national government.
cases.mechanism: A protest by a local council, with no effect on French sovereignty.

cases.name: Holy Empire of Reunion
cases.anchor: Réunion, the place parodied; the founders were in Brazil
cases.story: Brazilian law students created the Holy Empire of Reunion in 1997 as a parody of the French overseas department of Réunion.
cases.mechanism: A parody claim on a place that is part of France.

cases.name: Republic of Montmartre
cases.story: Proposed by cartoonist Jean Barrez in 1921, this Paris artists' association supports local artists, resists development in the area and does charity work.
cases.mechanism: An association using the form of a republic, with no separate status in French law.

cases.name: United Republics of Jämtland, Härjedalen and Ravund
cases.anchor: Östersund, placed for the region
cases.story: Founded in Sweden in 1963, this project bases its claim on Jämtland's autonomy before 1178 and aims to promote Jämtlandic culture.
cases.mechanism: A historical autonomy argument used for cultural promotion.

cases.name: Free Borough of Llanrwst
cases.story: Llanrwst in Wales was claimed as a free borough by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1276, a privilege defended for decades against the Church, and the list gives a second date of 1947.
cases.mechanism: A medieval local privilege, a different thing from a claim of statehood.

cases.name: Maritime Republic of Eastport
cases.story: The Annapolis, Maryland, neighborhood of Eastport declared independence in 1998 while a drawbridge closure cut it off, partly to promote local business.
cases.mechanism: A neighborhood's promotional declaration.

cases.name: Most Serene Federal Republic of Montmartre
cases.challenge: Phone book dispute at a New York state commission
cases.story: Dating from about 1965 and retroactively to 1636, this project claims Manhattan's Theater District. A dispute with New York Telephone over phone book listings reached a state commission.
cases.mechanism: The nearest it came to official notice was a utility dispute before a state commission.

cases.name: Zaqistan
cases.anchor: Center of Utah; the page names no site
cases.story: Zaqistan, founded in 2005, claims a small area in Utah.
cases.mechanism: A claim on land inside Utah, with no stated legal effect.

cases.name: Republic of Parva Domus Magna Quies
cases.story: This social organization in Punta Carretas, Montevideo, founded in 1878, calls itself a country. Its territory is one residence and its land.
cases.mechanism: A social club using the form of a republic.

cases.name: Sovereign Humanitarian Mission State of Aeterna Lucia
cases.anchor: New South Wales center; the page names no site
cases.story: Founded in New South Wales in 1978 and active to 1996, its founder claimed a baron's title from an exiled king. It moved twice within the state. A 1990 fraud charge was dropped.
cases.mechanism: A title claim from an exiled king gave no standing in Australian law.

cases.name: Province of Bumbunga
cases.anchor: South Australia near Lake Bumbunga, placed from general knowledge
cases.story: A monarchist in South Australia declared a farm independent in 1976, worried that Australia might become a republic, and stayed loyal to the Crown. It lasted until about 2000.
cases.mechanism: A secession to stay under the Crown, the reverse of the usual claim.

cases.name: Principality of Marlborough
cases.anchor: Marlborough, Queensland; site is inferred from the name
cases.story: In 1993 a family in Queensland declared independence after property was repossessed. Police evicted them after eleven days.
cases.mechanism: A declaration does not stop a repossession; police enforced it within eleven days.

cases.name: Independent State of Rainbow Creek
cases.anchor: Victoria; site inferred from the name
cases.story: Farmers in Victoria, Australia, seceded in 1979 in a dispute with the state over flood damage and taxes, inspired by Hutt River and staying loyal to the Crown. It lasted to the mid-1980s.
cases.mechanism: A farm secession modeled on Hutt River, with the same loyalty to the Crown.

cases.name: Kingdom of L'Anse-Saint-Jean
cases.story: This Quebec municipality voted to become a municipal monarchy in 1997, partly to boost tourism. It lasted until 2000.
cases.mechanism: A municipal vote for tourism with no effect on Canadian sovereignty.

cases.name: Kingdom of Vikesland
cases.founder: TV cameraman, not named on the page
cases.story: A television cameraman founded Vikesland in Brandon, Manitoba, in 2005 to document micronations. It claimed his residence and a nearby property until 2018.
cases.mechanism: A documentary subject that its own maker created.

cases.name: Republic of Peščenica
cases.story: TV talk-show host Željko Malnar declared this republic on his show in 1992, in a neighborhood of Zagreb, Croatia. It lasted to 2010.
cases.mechanism: A running television joke.

cases.name: Bunte Republik Neustadt
cases.story: The Bunte Republik Neustadt existed in Dresden, Germany, from 1990 to 1993. The list gives no more.
cases.mechanism: Listed without a stated claim or legal outcome.

cases.name: Rüterberg
cases.story: In 1989 the German village of Rüterberg declared independence. The Berlin Wall fell the next day and the village became part of reunified Germany.
cases.mechanism: A local declaration overtaken within a day by the collapse of the state it opposed.

cases.name: Keraton Agung Sejagat
cases.anchor: Purworejo from general knowledge; the page says Indonesia
cases.founder: Co-founder, not named on the page
cases.story: Started in Indonesia in 2018, it claimed dominion over the whole Earth under a supposed centuries-old agreement. Its co-founder later admitted the enterprise was fraudulent, and it ended in 2020.
cases.mechanism: Claims of a historic treaty collapsed when the founder admitted the fraud.

cases.name: Sunda Democratic Empire
cases.anchor: Bandung from general knowledge; the page says Indonesia
cases.story: Founded in Indonesia in 2003, its founder claimed to succeed Alexander the Great. He and two other leaders were imprisoned for spreading false information. It ended in 2020.
cases.mechanism: Indonesian authorities prosecuted the claim as false information.

cases.name: Republic of Malu Entu
cases.story: Sardinian separatists occupied the island of Mal di Ventre off Sardinia in 2008 and declared it independent. It ended in 2009.
cases.mechanism: An occupation of Italian territory to promote Sardinian separatism.

cases.name: Independent State of Aramoana
cases.story: A New Zealand community declared independence in 1980 to protest plans for an aluminium smelter nearby. It ended in 1981.
cases.mechanism: A protest declaration aimed at a proposed smelter.

cases.name: Sultanate of M'Simbati
cases.anchor: Msimbati, Tanzania, from general knowledge; the page says only Tanganyika
cases.founder: Founder, not named on the page
cases.story: In 1959 a man in Tanganyika declared his property independent and named himself sultan. The list gives it an end date of 1980.
cases.mechanism: A private estate's claim inside what is now Tanzania; the page gives no state response.

cases.name: Islands of Refreshment
cases.story: Jonathan Lambert declared himself ruler of Tristan da Cunha in 1811. The list ends the claim in 1816 and says the UK later annexed the island to prevent French or US use.
cases.mechanism: One man's occupation held only until a state annexed the island.

cases.name: Kingdom of Lovely
cases.anchor: East London; flat address not on the page
cases.story: Danny Wallace created Lovely in 2004 for a TV series, claiming his East London flat. It lasted to 2013.
cases.mechanism: A TV project with a flat as its territory.

cases.name: Principality of Freedonia
cases.story: College students started this libertarian project in 1997. It never acquired territory beyond one leader's home in Boston, and ended in 2004.
cases.mechanism: A libertarian plan that failed at the first step, buying land.

cases.name: Principality of Filettino
cases.story: The mayor of Filettino, Italy, created this principality in 2011 in protest at an austerity measure affecting small local governments.
cases.mechanism: A local protest against national austerity law.
